Week 39 · Weekend Recap & The Week Ahead · Sept 25–27, 2026

The Paradise Wins India.
Hanuman Ansh Clears ₹305 Cr.
And A Re-Release
Won America.

The Vvaan opens to ₹31 Cr · Drishyam sells 44,711 seats on day one · Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise, one week apart
Boxoffy Desk · Monday 28 September 2026

Four new films opened in India this weekend and none of them could shift a ₹2 crore devotional that has been in cinemas since August. In America, the biggest film of the weekend came out in 2019. And on Friday, two of the last movie stars alive open original films on the same date, in two different countries, both chasing numbers their own careers say are hard to reach.

The short version

Seven things worth knowing this morning.

Weekend of 25–27 September 2026 · Friday and Saturday actuals, Sunday estimated
The Paradise is India's number one film, with an estimated ₹46.15 crore for the weekend and ₹92.40 crore in four days, across Telugu, Hindi and Tamil.
The Vvaan opened to an estimated ₹31 crore — a genuine shock for a film Bollywood Hungama reported had been "largely dismissed as a non-starter by industry insiders" before release.
Hanuman Ansh has crossed ₹305 crore India net on day 52, and is still fourth in the country on an estimated ₹16.95 crore weekend.
Avengers: Endgame Encore is the number one film in America on a studio estimate near $26 million from 3,060 theatres — a seven-year-old re-release beating four new wide films.
Brad Pitt opened an original film to roughly $20 million on 87% from critics and an A− CinemaScore. Tom Cruise opens his on Friday, tracking at $20 million.
Drishyam: The Conclusion sold 44,711 national chain tickets on its first day of booking, at an unusually steep ₹453 a ticket.
Irumudi debuted at number three on Netflix's global non-English film chart with 3.4 million views off only three days of availability.

A word on the numbers here. Indian Friday and Saturday figures are settled actuals. Every Indian Sunday figure is our own estimate, and it is labelled as one — Sunday settles today and we will grade ourselves against it. American weekend figures are studio Sunday estimates, not actuals, and today will move them.
Grading ourselves

One call landed. Two we got wrong.

Hanuman Ansh, week seven. On 18 September we put its weekend at ₹26–34 crore. It came in at ₹28.50 crore — inside the band, and nearer the middle than the edge. We also called that weekend a miss on the Saturday, having read a live counter as a settled figure. It was not, and we retracted it. That mistake is the reason every Sunday number in this piece carries a label.

Our Drishyam opening day call was too low. We said ₹47 crore. That number rested on an assumption we had made up rather than measured — that a film's first day of booking accounts for about 15% of its final advance. Stree 2's actual booking history says 10%. Applied properly, Drishyam's 44,711 first-day tickets point to a finish above Stree 2's own record. We have moved to ₹55 crore, band ₹50–60.

And a correction on Tom Cruise. We have written before that Oblivion (2013) was Cruise's last original, non-franchise lead, opening at $38.2 million. Both halves were wrong. The $38.2 million was a Sunday estimate; the actual was $37.05 million. And Oblivion was not the last — Edge of Tomorrow and American Made both followed. His most recent original non-franchise lead is American Made, which opened at $16.78 million. That number matters on Friday, and it does not flatter our Digger call.

India · Weekend 25–27 September

Six of the top ten opened this week.

And a fifty-two-day-old film still finished fourth. That is the shape of the Indian weekend — a crowded slate of new arrivals, not one of which could move the film that has refused to leave since August.

Irumudi is missing from this chart, and that needs explaining. Ravi Teja's film has taken ₹190.10 crore in India, but daily tracking stopped on 23 September and nobody has published a figure for this weekend. It went to Netflix on 18 September, which is why the theatrical run ended as it did. We would rather leave a ₹190 crore film off a chart with a note than invent a number to fill the row.
Heart of the Beast and Dorothy are separated by ₹0.18 crore on our estimate, and by ₹0.02 crore on settled Friday and Saturday figures. Those two places are a coin flip until Sunday lands.
Number one

The Paradise, and what Nani has quietly become.

An estimated ₹46.15 crore weekend and ₹92.40 crore in four days makes The Paradise the biggest film in the country, and it got there off a Wednesday premiere and a Thursday wide release rather than a conventional Friday. The Telugu version is doing nearly all the work — of the first ₹78 crore, roughly ₹69 crore came from Telugu, ₹5 crore from Hindi and ₹1.65 crore from Tamil.

Sit with that split for a moment. This is a Telugu star opening a Telugu film to Telugu audiences at a scale that puts him first in India, with no need for a pan-India Hindi number to get him there. Box Office India called the Hindi version's opening day "decent," crossing ₹2 crore. The Hindi run is a bonus. It is not the engine.

Nani has spent a decade being described as the actor who works without the machinery — no franchise, no mass-hero template, no dependence on dubbed markets. This weekend he is number one in India ahead of a Hindi star vehicle, a Marvel re-release and a devotional phenomenon, and roughly nine rupees in every ten came from a single language.
The surprise

Sidharth Malhotra just had the second-biggest opening of his career.

An estimated ₹31 crore across three days is, by a distance, the best result of his recent career. His last four openers were Marjaavaan at ₹7.09 crore, Thank God at ₹7.38 crore, Yodha at ₹3.91 crore and Param Sundari at ₹6.85 crore. The Vvaan's Friday alone was ₹8.00 crore on Sacnilk, with Box Office India reading it a little lower at ₹7.50–7.75 crore.

What makes it remarkable is that nobody saw it coming. Bollywood Hungama's pre-release report described the film as "largely dismissed as a non-starter by industry insiders," and had final national chain pre-sales tracking to around 30,000 tickets — a modest number by any measure. Occupancy on the final advance was 11%. This film did not arrive with a weekend. It grew into one.

The catch is the calendar. Drishyam: The Conclusion takes the screens on Friday, which leaves The Vvaan exactly one clean week. Malhotra's opening-to-lifetime multiplier has a median near 6.2x across his career, but the films that ran into a big second-week release converted worst — Thank God at 4.47x, Baar Baar Dekho at 4.52x. On a clash-constrained multiplier, ₹31 crore points somewhere into the ₹130–155 crore range. That would still be the second-biggest film he has made.

The story of the year

₹305 crore, on a ₹2 crore budget, on day 52.

There is no modern Hindi comparison for what Hanuman Ansh is doing. It opened small. It has never been the loudest film in the country. And it has now earned more than 150 times its production budget while still pulling an estimated ₹16.95 crore in its eighth weekend — more than every new Tamil, Malayalam and English release this week put together, Meesaya Murukku 2 aside.

Our 18 September preview put its seventh weekend at ₹26–34 crore, and it landed at ₹28.50 crore. The eighth is down about 41% on that, which is the first real deceleration the film has shown. But it is decelerating from a height almost nothing in Hindi cinema reaches, and it is doing so against three new releases and a re-release all taking screens at once.

The honest read is that this is no longer a film that is holding. It is a film that is finishing, slowly, from very high up. ₹320 crore is comfortably in range. ₹350 would need another holiday weekend, and Friday belongs to Drishyam.
The week ahead · 2 October

Drishyam sold 44,711 seats in a day, and it is outrunning Stree 2.

Advance bookings opened on Sunday, five days before release. By the afternoon the film had sold 21,098 tickets across PVR, INOX and Cinepolis. By midnight it had 44,711 — it more than doubled inside the day.

The number that jumps out is not the count. It is the price. ₹453 per ticket on the national chains, against a market running closer to ₹280. That is a 62% premium on a standard-format 2D thriller with no IMAX and no premium screens anywhere in its release. A holiday Friday and a franchise finale will do that.

Why we moved our number

Stree 2 holds the record for the cheapest ₹50 crore opening in Hindi cinema — 3.92 lakh chain tickets for a ₹53.12 crore day one. It also got exactly the same five-day booking window Drishyam has, which makes the two directly comparable.

Stree 2 · 2024Drishyam 3 · 2026
First day of selling~40,00044,711
Time taken~24 hours~14 hours
Day one as share of final10.2%—
Final chain tickets3.92 lakh~4.4 lakh projected
India day one₹53.12 Cr₹55 Cr call

Stree 2 needed close to twenty-four hours to reach 40,000 tickets. Drishyam got to 44,711 in about fourteen. More tickets, ten hours less. And Stree 2's first day of selling turned out to be just 10.2% of everything it eventually sold — not the 15% we had assumed. Run Drishyam's 44,711 through that shape and it finishes near 4.4 lakh, above what Stree 2 managed. The distribution plan helps too: around 18,000 shows on day one in India, which is roughly what Stree 2 and Jawan carried at their peak. A film needs the screens before it can sell the seats, and this one has them.

North America, counted seat by seat

Nobody publishes overseas presales for Hindi films, so we went and counted them. Across five showtimes in two markets, 41 of 366 seats were sold — 11.2% — about a day into North American sales.

Cinemark Allen 16Allen, TX10:00pm5 / 746.8%$13.50
Cinemark Allen 16Allen, TX11:45am5 / 746.8%$10.50
Cinemark Dallas XDDallas, TX7:55pm2 / 543.7%$13.50

Three things came out of that count that no advance report will give you. The auditoriums are small — 54 to 102 seats; Cinemark has given this film four to five showtimes a site and then put it in its smallest rooms, so if it performs, the ceiling is the room and not the audience. The Bay Area is paying 24% more a ticket than Dallas. And every booking so far is a contiguous block of two to seven seats in the centre rows. Those are families, not bulk buys.

Los Angeles has no Cinemark screens for this film at all. Cinemark is playing Drishyam on five sites in Dallas and five in the Bay Area. In LA metro, zero — the nearest Cinemark screen showing it to Orange County is 327 miles away in San Jose. Regal is not carrying the film nationally. AMC is giving it one showtime a site.

And the rest of the world

We counted those too. In the UAE, VOX has 71 showtimes across 12 sites on opening day. Saudi Arabia gets it across six cities, but rated 18TC against the PG15 it carries in the Emirates. Canada has it at 32 Landmark locations. Australia has a date at Event and HOYTS but the film is not classified yet, so no sessions are on sale. The UK has it booked in at Vue with no showtimes up.

And there is no Thursday premiere in any market. Not the Gulf, not America, not Australia — every listing begins on Friday. Drishyam 2's Gulf opening day included Thursday shows. This one does not get them.

Which is why we have cut our overseas number from $9.7 million to $7.5 million, band $6.5–8.5. Drishyam 2 did $7.22 million overseas, the biggest international run of Ajay Devgn's career. The franchise has got bigger. The overseas footprint has not.
United States · Weekend 25–27 September

The number one film in America came out in 2019.

Avengers: Endgame Encore — a re-release carrying two to four minutes of new footage setting up Avengers: Doomsday — is the top film in the United States on a studio estimate near $26 million from 3,060 theatres. It did $3.8 million in Thursday previews and $11.2 million on Friday, and pushes Endgame's running domestic lifetime to roughly $884 million.

These are provisional. Every figure above is a studio Sunday estimate and today's actuals will move them. Places six to ten had not been published anywhere we can reach at the time of writing. Deadline's own headline for the frame was "Four Films Eye $20M+ Each," which is the shape of the weekend even where the decimals are not settled.

Resident Evil fell off a cliff

A 60% second-weekend drop, from $60.15 million to roughly $23.8 million, on a film holding 96% on Rotten Tomatoes across 121 reviews — the best-reviewed video game adaptation ever made. Box Office Pro had it holding at $25–30 million on word of mouth. It did not. The reviews bought it an opening. They did not buy it a second weekend.

Brad Pitt opened an original film to $20 million and 87%

Heart of the Beast — directed by David Ayer, with Pitt as a Special Forces veteran, produced through his own Plan B — opened to an estimated $20 million from 3,435 theatres, on 87% from critics, 94% from audiences, a Metacritic of 65 and an A− CinemaScore. That is an original, non-franchise, star-led film opening cleanly in a market that is constantly told it can no longer do that.

Pitt's own record gives it scale. F1 opened at $57.00 million last year and finished at $189.64 million domestic, the biggest film of his career worldwide. Bullet Train opened at $30.03 million. Ad Astra at $19.00 million. Babylon at $3.60 million. Twenty million for a mid-budget original thriller with these reviews is a solid result, not a soft one.
The week ahead · 2 October

Digger, and the gap between our call and the tracking.

Alejandro G. Iñárritu's Digger, with Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell, opens Friday from Warner Bros. R-rated, 128 minutes, shot on 35mm VistaVision by Emmanuel Lubezki, with Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Jesse Plemons and Michael Stuhlbarg around him. IMAX is confirmed, though the format allocation has not been published.

We have this film at $32 million. Almost nobody else does. NRG's tracking, via Matthew Belloni, has it near $20 million. Box Office Theory has $23.5 million. Box Office Pro's long-range band is $20–30 million. We sit above all of them, and it is worth saying plainly why that is now uncomfortable.

FilmDomestic openDomestic total
Top Gun: Maverick2022 · franchise$126.71M$718.73M

The pattern is unmistakable, and it is not about Cruise. It is about the franchise. Inside one, he opens at $64 million or $127 million. Outside one, his last three readings are $37.05 million, $28.76 million and $16.78 million, descending across twelve years. Digger is outside one.

Iñárritu's own record points the same way. He has gone wide exactly once, with The Revenant, which opened at $39.80 million. Killers of the Flower Moon, the closest comparison in prestige, length and awards positioning, opened at $23.0 million. Reviews remain the unknown — no Metascore or Tomatometer has been published, and The Hollywood Reporter described premiere reactions as "very mixed."

Share this WhatsApp X Facebook Telegram
Our tripwires were set before the weekend and two are now live: Thursday previews under $2.5 million, a soft IMAX and PLF Friday, or a Rotten Tomatoes score under 65%. With tracking at $20 million and reactions reported as split, $32 million asks the film to beat its own tracking by 60%. We are holding the call. We are not defending it comfortably.
Streaming · Week of 14–20 September

A Tamil-Telugu film went to Netflix and charted worldwide in three days.

Irumudi arrived on Netflix on 18 September in five languages, giving it three days inside the measurement week. It debuted at number three on the global non-English films chart with 3.4 million views, second in India behind Vishwanath & Sons, and by the daily chart of 26 September it had climbed to number one in India. A full week at that rate would have contested the global non-English top spot outright.

India, and a record only cricket had held

Bigg Boss season 20 crossed 20 million Ormax views in the week ending 20 September — the first non-cricket property all year to clear 20 million in a single week, up from 16.8 million in its opening week. For scale, the top title in an ordinary August week, an India–Sri Lanka Test series, managed 7.5 million.

Two more movers worth a line. The Gentlemen season two is collapsing against season one — 22.6 million cumulative views at the equivalent point against 44.0 million, down 49% — while season one re-entered the chart at number five. And Crew Girl's hours jumped almost 120% week-on-week after Netflix announced a second season, which is a rare case of a renewal moving the numbers rather than following them.
What to watch

Two stars, one Friday, two countries.

On 2 October, Ajay Devgn closes a franchise in India while Tom Cruise opens an original in America, on the same date, both needing numbers their own histories say are hard. Drishyam needs somewhere near 4.4 lakh national chain tickets for the ₹55 crore day we have called. Cruise needs to clear his own non-franchise ceiling by a wide margin. Neither is impossible. Neither happens by default.

Method

Where these numbers come from.

Indian collections follow the Boxoffy Calibration Model's twelve approved sources, with Box Office India taking precedence, then Sacnilk, then Bollywood Hungama. American figures come from The Numbers, Box Office Pro, Box Office Theory and Comscore-derived studio estimates. Streaming figures come from Netflix's own Tudum charts, Nielsen and Ormax Media. Seat-level occupancy for Drishyam in North America, and the showtime counts for the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Canada and Australia, were counted directly from exhibitor listings on 27 and 28 September.

Friday and Saturday Indian figures are settled actuals. Sunday Indian figures are our estimates and are labelled throughout. American weekend figures are studio Sunday estimates and are labelled throughout. Where a figure is not published, we say so rather than estimating it — which is why Irumudi's weekend is absent, why five places on the American chart are blank, and why no runtime for Drishyam appears anywhere in this piece. Six sources give six different ones.
